s1_hook: College soccer teams film their games from the stands, on a phone. Touchline AI turns that footage into tactical analysis, like team shape and heatmaps. But it also does something most tools don't. It checks whether its own numbers can be trusted.
s2_upload: A coach uploads a short clip. OpenCV 5 decodes every frame straight away, to check the length, the resolution, and that the video is actually readable.
s3_wrong: Next comes calibration. The coach clicks four points of a known pitch area. Clicked in the wrong order, the tool refuses, and explains why. It never guesses.
s3_right: In the right order, the calibration is accepted. These magenta lines are the entire pitch, projected back through those four points, so it's easy to see whether the geometry makes sense.
s4_run: Running the analysis sends the job to AWS. A worker on EC2 pulls the clip from S3, detects every player with a model running on OpenCV's DNN module, tracks them, and maps them onto a top-down pitch. This takes a few minutes, so let's jump to a finished run.
s5_agent: Here is the heart of the project. For every four seconds of video, an agent checks its own work. In segment two, the phone drifted a hundred and thirty-four pixels from where it was calibrated, so the painted lines no longer line up. Alignment dropped to zero point two. The camera-motion estimate is reliable, so the agent decides to re-estimate the motion and update the calibration. It reruns only this segment, and compares before and after on the same frames. Alignment rises to zero point eight two, so it keeps the fix. If a fix doesn't validate, it keeps the original result, flags the segment, and asks the coach. And it never retries more than twice.
s6_proof: Here is the same frame, before and after. Without the correction, the lines slide off the pitch. With it, they lock back on. In the video, you can flip between the two runs.
s7_tactics: With the geometry fixed, the top-down view and heatmap can be trusted. Team width and depth are labelled as visible players only. And the app is upfront about what it does not measure. Possession, passing and speed are listed as not measured, instead of invented.
s8_results: On real footage, and on stress tests like fast pans, sped-up video and a scene cut, it picked the right action in eight of nine cases. After the camera moved, position error dropped from seven point nine metres to zero point six. And it all runs on AWS. These are the files the EC2 worker wrote to S3.
s9_close: Touchline AI. Analysis that knows when it's wrong. Try the recorded run online, and find all the code on GitHub.
